energy_regime.note: Low-energy end from the DeepCore threshold of about 10 GeV on the same page.
energy_regime.quote: IceTop, built as a veto and calibration detector for IceCube, also detects air showers from primary cosmic rays in the 300 TeV to 1 EeV energy range.
energy_regime.value: About 10 GeV (DeepCore threshold) to the PeV scale and above for in-ice neutrinos; 300 TeV to 1 EeV cosmic rays with IceTop

facility_roles.quote: IceCube, the South Pole neutrino observatory, is a cubic-kilometer particle detector made of Antarctic ice and located near the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.

intervals.label: proposal
intervals.note: 67-page proposal to the NSF and to partners in Belgium, Germany and Sweden.
intervals.quote: In November 1999, the fledgling IceCube Collaboration (mostly members of the AMANDA Collaboration) submitted a 67-page proposal for a cubic-kilometer neutrino detector at the South Pole to the US National Science Foundation and to partners in Belgium, Germany, and Sweden.

intervals.label: first NSB award
intervals.note: $15 M approved in March 2002; up to $24.54 M followed in May 2003. NSF eventually contributed $242 M of a $279 M total project cost.
intervals.quote: the National Science Board (NSB), the 24-member policy body for the National Science Foundation (NSF), approved a $15 million award for the IceCube project.

intervals.label: construction
intervals.note: Seven austral summers, November to February, from 2004 until 2011; one string (#21) in the 2004 season, the last of 86 on 18 December 2010.
intervals.quote: On December 18, 2010, just after 6 pm New Zealand time, the last of IceCube’s 86 strings was lowered into the Antarctic ice.

intervals.label: partial-detector operation and commissioning
intervals.note: IceCube took data with partial configurations from 2005; the detector paper states “Construction was completed on December 18, 2010, and commissioning was completed in 2011.” End is recorded at month precision because only the 13 May 2011 start of full operation is published.
intervals.quote: Though IceCube had been taking data since 2005, it didn’t begin full operations until May 13, 2011, when the detector took its first set of data as a completed instrument.

intervals.label: IC86 physics runs
intervals.note: Full 86-string operation; “Since then, IceCube has collected data continuously.”
intervals.quote: Though IceCube had been taking data since 2005, it didn’t begin full operations until May 13, 2011, when the detector took its first set of data as a completed instrument.

quantity.quote: The IceCube detector is one cubic kilometer of ice—that would be enough water to fill one million swimming pools.
The in-ice component of IceCube consists of 5,160 digital optical modules (DOMs), each with a ten-inch photomultiplier tube and associated electronics.
The DOMs are attached to vertical “strings,” frozen into 86 boreholes and arrayed over a cubic kilometer from 1,450 meters to 2,450 meters depth.
DOMs are attached to the cables beginning at a depth of 1,450 meter and ending at a depth of 2,450 meters.
IceTop consists of 81 stations located on top of the same number of IceCube strings. Each station has two tanks, each equipped with two downward facing DOMs.

lineage.note: AMANDA was the in-ice proof of concept and merged into the IceCube Collaboration on 20 March 2005.
lineage.quote: On March 20, 2005, after nine years of operation, AMANDA officially became part of IceCube!

name: IceCube
notes: The ontology's experiment-kind enum has no “indirect_dark_matter” value, so IceCube's indirect dark-matter search programme is recorded in physics_goals and in topic:indirect-dark-matter-detection rather than in secondary_kinds.

Per-season string deployment counts (IC1/IC9/IC22/IC40/IC59/IC79/IC86) could not be sourced: neither the official pages nor the JINST detector paper as fetched publish a per-season table. Only the 2004 first string (#21), the 18 December 2010 final string and the seven-season span are recorded.

Funding: “The IceCube Neutrino Observatory was built under a National Science Foundation (NSF) Major Research Equipment and Facilities Construction grant”; the University of Wisconsin–Madison is the lead institution for maintenance and operations.

physics_goals.quote: IceCube is the first gigaton neutrino detector ever built and was primarily designed to observe neutrinos from the most violent astrophysical sources in our universe.
physics_goals.value: Observe high-energy neutrinos from the most violent astrophysical sources and identify their origins

physics_goals.quote: IceCube collaborators address several big questions in physics, like the nature of dark matter and the properties of the neutrino itself. IceCube also observes cosmic rays that interact with the Earth’s atmosphere, which have revealed fascinating structures that are not presently understood.
physics_goals.value: Probe the nature of dark matter

physics_goals.quote: This denser configuration forms the DeepCore subdetector, which lowers the neutrino energy threshold to about 10 GeV, creating the opportunity to study neutrino oscillations.
physics_goals.value: Measure the properties of the neutrino itself, including atmospheric neutrino oscillations

physics_goals.quote: The surface array measures the cosmic-ray arrival directions in the Southern Hemisphere as well as the flux and composition of cosmic rays.
physics_goals.value: Measure cosmic rays interacting in the Earth's atmosphere, including their flux, composition and arrival directions

summary.plain: A cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice at the South Pole turned into a telescope. More than five thousand light sensors frozen deep in the ice catch the faint flashes made when a neutrino from space crashes into the ice.
summary.technical: Gigaton-scale in-ice Cherenkov neutrino observatory: 5,160 DOMs on 86 strings between 1,450 m and 2,450 m depth on a 125 m hexagonal grid, with the DeepCore infill (threshold ~10 GeV) and the 81-station IceTop surface air-shower array. Full 86-string operation since 13 May 2011; discovered the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux and identified TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane as neutrino sources.

unique_capabilities.quote: IceCube, the only cubic-kilometer neutrino detector constructed to date, was completed in December 2010, only six years after the deployment of the first string at the South Pole.
unique_capabilities.value: The first and only cubic-kilometre (gigaton) neutrino detector built to date

unique_capabilities.quote: The Antarctic neutrino observatory, which also includes the surface array IceTop and the dense infill array DeepCore, was designed as a multipurpose experiment.
unique_capabilities.value: A multipurpose observatory combining the deep in-ice array with the IceTop surface air-shower array and the DeepCore low-energy infill
